title: latency-first-poc-hosting-experiment-plan
summary: Experiment plan to validate a latency-first hosting recommendation for a mid-market customer with strict P95 SLOs. Compares hosted, dedicated and private deployment options via staged synthetic + pilot tests; includes measurement plan, rollback/fallback routing, and per-mode runbooks.
body:
Purpose:
This doc captures a concrete, runnable experiment plan to determine the hosting recommendation for Customer X (mid-market ecommerce platform). The primary objective is to validate whether Redwood Hosted, Redwood Dedicated, or a Private (VPC) deployment meets the customer’s hard P95 latency SLO (<= 120ms end-to-end for text-completion API on 1k token prompts) while remaining within acceptable monthly cost and operational effort.

Context and constraints:
- Customer profile: serves interactive product recommendation and chat experiences; steady 50 QPS during peak, spiky bursts to 250 QPS for short windows; must keep 99.9% availability during business hours; data residency in eu-west-1 required.
- Primary metric: inference P95 (end-to-end request latency measured at application edge). Secondary metrics: P50/P99, error rate, cold-start frequency, cache hit ratio, cost per 1M tokens, and operational MTTD for incidents.
- Workload characteristics: prompt lengths ~600–1,200 tokens (mostly 800), 60% of requests follow repeated prefixes (good cache locality), 70% of calls are single-turn completion; roughly 30% of requests call external tooling for enrichment (adds 20–50ms pre/post processing).

Success criteria (pass/fail):
- Pass: P95 <= 120ms for 95% of test windows in steady-state and during a defined spike test (see below); error rate <0.5%; total monthly cost delta between modes within acceptable band (TBD by FinOps).
- Fail: Any deployment option that cannot achieve the P95 target with engineering config changes (batching, quantization) and routing policy without exceeding an agreed cost threshold or unacceptable operational risk.

Experiment overview (three pillars):
1) Synthetic lab: microbenching and kernel-level profiling to measure baseline latencies per-token, attention scaling, and cold-start behavior across target instance types (A6000-equivalent and H100-equivalent).
2) Staging canary: run realistic traffic replay against three isolated environments (hosted, dedicated pool, private VPC) using the same model version + quantization profile. Capture end-to-end measurements via distributed tracing.
3) Beta shadow/cutover: route 10–15% of live traffic to selected configuration for 48–72 hours with automatic fallback to primary route on SLO breach.

Detailed test matrix:
- Variables: model variant (fp16, 4-bit), kernel selection (fast-attn vs general), batching window (0ms, 10ms, 30ms), KV cache enabled/disabled, region placement (eu-west-1 vs fallback eu-west-3), instance family (A100/RTX6000 vs H100).
- For each combination capture: P50/P95/P99, tail-latency percentile histograms, token throughput, GPU utilization, batch size distribution, cache hit ratio, and cold-start count.
- Spike test: ramp from 50 QPS to 250 QPS over 60s, hold 180s, then drop; repeated 3x per run.

Runbook per hosting mode (high-level):
- Hosted: use Redwood Hosted endpoints in eu-west-1. Configure autoscaling target with strict min instances to avoid cold start. Enable prefix/KV cache and continuous warm pools. Implement traffic shaping policy: 95% to hosted primary, 5% to hosted-staging (for monitoring).
- Dedicated: reserve a dedicated GPU pool sized for expected peak with burst headroom. Deploy model with aggressive micro-batching disabled; configure autoscaler with fast scale-up and slower scale-down. Pin model version and enable intra-pool warm caches.
- Private (VPC): deploy private control-plane bundle in customer VPC. Prefer H100 nodes for latency-critical single-token steps. Accept additional networking latency (vpn/expressroute) in measurement plan; include an NTP and tracing alignment step.

Estimated one-time and monthly cost rough numbers (ballpark for sizing conversation):
- Hosted: lower ops cost, medium per-token cost. Estimated incremental monthly infra cost: $12k–$18k for this workload band.
- Dedicated: higher baseline reservation cost but lower unit cost at sustained scale. Estimated monthly committed cost: $22k–$32k depending on instance family and burst buffer.
- Private: highest integration and licensing effort; infra cost similar to dedicated plus managed-support uplift. Estimated monthly baseline: $28k–$40k plus integration professional services.
(These numbers are starting points for FinOps; actual quotes will be produced after confirmed instance selection and network egress estimates.)

Measurement instrumentation and dashboards:
- Traces: add a high-cardinality tag for routing decision and model variant. Record edge->platform->gpu time steps.
- Metrics: p95_latency_ms, p99_latency_ms, error_rate, tokens_per_second, avg_batch_size, cache_hit_ratio, cold_start_rate, cost_per_1M_tokens (estimated).
- Dashboards: per-mode dashboards and a cross-mode comparison board. Include waterfall trace views for slow requests.

Fallback and graceful degradation plan:
- Primary fallback: automatic routing policy to a cheaper model variant or a replica region when P95 crosses 150ms for >2 min.
- Circuit breaker: if error_rate >1% or cold_start_rate spikes >3x baseline for 5 min then route traffic to alternative hosting mode (pre-wired in the routing policy).

Workshop-derived design notes (synthesis of workshop held 2025-11-20):
- Observations: customer’s prefix locality suggests high cache benefits; initial microbench shows 40–60ms of GPU time dominated by KV lookup for long sequences.
- Decisions during workshop: prioritize Hosted for time-to-value while validating Dedicated for long-term cost; keep Private as fallback for customers requiring air-gapped or on-prem.
- Known risks: network variability for Private path, longer procurement for Dedicated reserved capacity, and potential model version drift between environments.

Open questions and data required:
- Exact FinOps threshold for monthly infra spend that customer is willing to accept (ask sales to confirm).
- Legal confirmation on egress/cross-border artifacts for eu-west-1 (security/compliance).
- Confirm whether external enrichment calls can be co-located or must remain off-cluster (affects end-to-end measurement).

Next steps and owners (short action list):
- Synthetic lab run (owner: Diego) – complete kernel-level bench matrix by 2025-11-26.
- Staging canary deployment (owner: Priya) – deploy three isolated test endpoints and enable tracing by 2025-12-03.
- Cost-model update (owner: Omar / FinOps) – map instance family choices to price bands and return a delta table by 2025-12-07.
- Legal check (owner: Ellen) – confirm data residency and egress constraints by 2025-11-28.
- Customer sync (owner: Maya) – present experiment plan and confirm acceptance criteria by 2025-11-18.

Appendix A — quick tuning checklist to try if P95 is high:
- Ensure KV/prefix cache warmup: pre-seed cache with most common prefixes before beta.
- Reduce batching window to 0–10ms for latency-sensitive traffic slice; use small-batch fast-path kernels.
- Try 4-bit quantization for inference to reduce compute latency; measure quality impact against evaluation set.
- Place endpoints in same AZ as customer ingress (eu-west-1 AZ alignment) to reduce network hop variability.

Appendix B — workshop notes raw points (snippets):
- "Customer worried about tail latency during flash sales; willing to pay for lower tail but needs fallback for failures."
- "Consider hybrid routing: hosted for baseline, dedicated for peak-offload, private for regulated flows."
- "SRE asked for a pre-authorized on-call runbook for canary rollback; engineering to supply playbook."

Notes on uniqueness: this doc focuses explicitly on a latency-first experimental plan with a concrete three-stage test approach, per-mode runbooks, and a set of controllable kernel/batch/caching variables. It is intentionally prescriptive (action owners, dates, spike profiles) to be directly runnable by solutions engineering and SRE teams.

End of document.
